hook: Betting that Modi will simply age out ignores how voters actually behave. Replacing a proven brand requires a credible upgrade, not an unproven alternative waiting passively on the shelf.
summary:
Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy frames the prime ministership as a routine retail cycle, arguing that Narendra Modi will reach his natural expiry date by 2029. Under this logic, power should automatically fall into Rahul Gandhi’s lap. But democratic elections are not automatic shelf cleanouts. By conceding that the incumbent is a working product, the opposition accidentally exposes its own deepest flaw: hoping to inherit the mandate instead of earning it.

Consumers do not dump a tested product for an untested brand out of sheer boredom. When everyday buyers seek a replacement, they look for dependable quality, not a discounted experiment that has gathered dust across two decades of election cycles. Expecting voters to turn toward a perennial second choice by default is a lethal miscalculation.

Modi’s tenure will eventually close, but political vacuums reward battle-tested muscle, not passive entitlement. If the opposition cannot offer a razor-sharp, compelling vision that commands immediate public confidence, the electorate will simply search for a fresh leader crafted in the incumbent's mold rather than rescue a brand that never proved it works.

summary:
Elon Musk is lashing out at Indian telecom leaders like Mukesh Ambani and Sunil Mittal, claiming they are choking off Starlink to protect their profits. He portrays his satellite network as a savior for underserved communities that supposedly cannot afford modern digital connectivity. But that story falls flat when you look at the real numbers across the country.

Over the past decade, Indian telecom operators completely rebuilt the digital landscape from scratch, dropping data costs down to some of the cheapest rates on the planet. Millions of citizens got fast internet because domestic providers invested heavily in grassroots infrastructure. Accessibility is no longer an urgent crisis waiting for a foreign billionaire's rescue.

Musk's frustration comes down to simple business reality. If Starlink actually wants to thrive in India's massive digital ecosystem, it needs to cooperate with trusted local institutions instead of trying to bulldoze through existing regulations.
